Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Where do the granny walking a hippo and the shark in trainers come from? If odd computer-made pictures and clips have reached your phone through family chats, you are not alone. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • More big American banks tell customers: if you let an AI assistant into your account, the losses are yours. Citibank, one of the largest American banks, has changed its rules: a customer who gives an outside AI assistant access to their account answers for everything that assistant does, even if it is hacked. The two largest US banks did the same in October, and two more followed this week. The banks point to the risk, but they also do not want an outside program standing between them and their customers. The advice is the same everywhere: never give your banking password to a program. Read more and the background.
  • More than half the electricity for America’s biggest data centers comes from gas and coal, a Harvard study finds. Researchers at Harvard counted 403 very large data centers in the United States from satellite pictures and estimated where their electricity comes from. More than half comes from burning gas and coal, and the resulting emissions are about as large as those of the whole of Denmark. The count stops in spring 2025, and much has been built since. The International Energy Agency expects data-center emissions worldwide to more than double by 2035, partly because American companies are building their own gas power plants so as not to wait for a grid connection. Read more and the background.
  • Russian linguists and doctors use AI to prepare reading texts for adults relearning to speak after a stroke. After a stroke, people often have to learn to speak again, and one of the exercises is reading and retelling simple texts. But almost all such texts are written for children. Linguists from the Higher School of Economics in St Petersburg and doctors from Krasnoyarsk taught an AI to simplify adult texts, such as news, history and gardening, at three levels of difficulty, and assembled 134 of them. It is early work: the texts were tried with 12 patients, and whether they speed up recovery has not been measured yet. Read more and the background.
  • Nvidia, the main maker of AI chips, stops selling to China. Nvidia, the American company that makes most of the chips for AI, has announced that it will stop selling chips to China. Until now one model could be sold there under a special arrangement with the US government. The decision came a week after the company’s long-time head stepped down and a day after a new American rule that closes China’s roundabout ways of getting such chips. The company says its revenue will not suffer, because there are more orders than it can fill. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Microsoft shows seven AI models of its own, cheaper than those of its partner OpenAI, Amazon and Google will together own nearly 30% of Anthropic once its shares are sold to the public, A detector says a prize-winning Peruvian novel is 99% machine-written; the publisher stands by its author, Google’s AI search gets a mode for questions you would rather not have remembered.

Answer to the question of the day. They are a new kind of folklore, argues the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok. The first picture-making programs made typical mistakes: extra fingers, wax-like faces. People did not just laugh at these; they turned them into a style. That is how the nonsense creatures came about: Tralalero Tralala, a shark in trainers, or Bombardiro Crocodilo. In 2025 Russian-language social networks filled with clips of an elderly woman walking her pet hippopotamus, Bulka; in later versions the hippo became a capybara or a crocodile, while the granny, the block of flats and the puddles in the yard stayed the same. The author points out that such jokes have every mark of folklore: they exist in many variants, they are made collectively, nobody knows the author, and they are built from stock images everyone recognises. As with a joke told at the table, the audience decides what survives: a picture that makes nobody laugh, shudder or go “aww” simply is not passed on. The program offers what is most typical and recognisable, and people pick and spread it. So who is the author: the person who typed the request, the thousands who remade it, or the program? The article’s answer is that there is no single author, just as with a folk tale. It adds a more serious note: as machine-made pictures become harder to tell from real ones, laughing at the obviously absurd ones may be a way of coping with the unease. Sistemny Blok, “‘This is my Bulka…’: how AI memes are becoming the new folklore” (June 2026) (article in Russian).
